author: Boethius
title: The Consolation of Philosophy, Book I
primary_pairs: Sad › Depressed / Inferior; Scared › Helpless / Insignificant
secondary_pairs: Mad › Hurt / Distant; Peaceful › Thoughtful / Pensive
key_line: For awhile he has forgotten himself; he will easily recover his memory
extract:
Who wrought my studious numbers
Smoothly once in happier days,
Now perforce in tears and sadness
Learn a mournful strain to raise.
Lo, the Muses, grief-dishevelled,
Guide my pen and voice my woe;
Down their cheeks unfeigned the tear drops
To my sad complainings flow!

[...] While I was thus mutely pondering within myself, and recording my sorrowful complainings with my pen, it seemed to me that there appeared above my head a woman of a countenance exceeding venerable. Her eyes were bright as fire, and of a more than human keenness. [...]

'There is no danger; these are the symptoms of lethargy, the usual sickness of deluded minds. For awhile he has forgotten himself; he will easily recover his memory, if only he first recognises me. And that he may do so, let me now wipe his eyes that are clouded with a mist of mortal things.' Thereat, with a fold of her robe, she dried my eyes all swimming with tears.
source: trans. H. R. James (1897), Project Gutenberg #14328 | Book I, Song I (opening lines); Prose I; Prose II

author: Seneca the Younger
title: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 28 ('On Travel as a Cure for Discontent')
secondary_pairs: Scared › Confused / Bewildered; Scared › Anxious / Overwhelmed
key_line: You need to change your soul, not your sky.
extract: Do you think this has happened to you alone? Are you surprised, as if it were something new, that after such a long journey and so many changes of scene you still haven't shaken off the gloom and heaviness in your mind? You need to change your soul, not your sky. [...] The same thing that drove you away is still pressing on you. What good can new lands do? Or getting to know new cities and places? All that rushing about comes to nothing. You ask why running away isn't helping? You are taking yourself with you.
source: Translated for this project from the Latin (Epistulae Morales 28.1-2) | Letter 28, sections 1-2
notes: Translation is ours, so no rights issue. Latin text checked against two online transcriptions.

author: Heloise d'Argenteuil
title: Heloise's first letter to Abelard
primary_pairs: Mad › Hurt / Distant; Sad › Lonely / Isolated
key_line: when I receive any letter from you I shall know you still remember me.
extract:
A consolatory letter of yours to a friend happened some days since to fall into my hands; my knowledge of the writing and my love of the hand gave me the curiosity to open it. [...] What reflections did I not make! I began to consider the whole afresh, and perceived myself pressed with the same weight of grief as when we first began to be miserable. Though length of time ought to have closed up my wounds, yet the seeing them described by your hand was sufficient to make them all open and bleed afresh. [...]

Write to me then immediately and wait not for miracles; they are too scarce, and we too much accustomed to misfortunes to expect a happy turn. I shall always have this, if you please, and this will always be agreeable to me, that when I receive any letter from you I shall know you still remember me.
source: The Love Letters of Abelard and Heloise (Seymour, 1903; reprinting the 1722 English version), Project Gutenberg #40227 | Heloise's first letter to Abelard
notes: This 18th-century English version is a loose rendering (via French), not a close translation of the Latin. Say 'from an 18th-century English version' in the app.

author: Christine de Pizan
title: The Book of the City of Ladies, opening chapters
primary_pairs: Scared › Insecure / Embarrassed; Scared › Submissive / Inadequate
secondary_pairs: Sad › Depressed / Inferior; Powerful › Faithful / Confident
extract: [A retelling, not a quotation] Christine is sitting in her study, surrounded by books, when she picks up a volume that insults women. She can't stop thinking about it. So many famous, learned men have said such things, she reasons, that they must be right, and she begins to despise herself and every woman she knows. In that low moment a light falls across her lap, and three crowned women appear: Reason, Rectitude and Justice. Reason tells her gently to stop believing the worst about herself just because powerful people have said it. Then they invite her to build something with them: a city, made of the stories of women who proved those men wrong.
source: Our own retelling of Book I, chapters 1-3 (no PD English translation suitable for quoting) | Book I, chapters 1-3
notes: Must be labelled as a retelling in the app. Could be replaced later with the team's own translation from the Middle French.

author: John Keats
title: Journal-letter to George and Georgiana Keats ('the vale of Soul-making')
date: 21 April 1819 (part of a letter written Feb-May 1819)
secondary_pairs: Joyful › Hopeful / Optimistic; Powerful › Aware / Surprised
key_line: Do you not see how necessary a World of Pains and troubles is to school an Intelligence and make it a soul?
extract: The common cognomen of this world among the misguided and superstitious is "a vale of tears," from which we are to be redeemed by a certain arbitrary interposition of God and taken to Heaven--What a little circumscribed straightened notion! Call the world if you please "The vale of Soul-making." Then you will find out the use of the world [...] There may be intelligences or sparks of the divinity in millions--but they are not Souls till they acquire identities, till each one is personally itself. [...] Do you not see how necessary a World of Pains and troubles is to school an Intelligence and make it a soul? A Place where the heart must feel and suffer in a thousand diverse ways.
source: Letters of John Keats to His Family and Friends, ed. Sidney Colvin (1891), Project Gutenberg #35698 | Letter to George and Georgiana Keats, Feb 14 - May 3 1819 (entry of 21 April)

author: Vincent van Gogh
title: Letter to Theo van Gogh, June 1880
primary_pairs: Sad › Lonely / Isolated; Scared › Rejected / Discouraged
key_line: There may be a great fire in our soul, but no one ever comes to warm himself by it
extract:
As a result one cannot rid oneself of melancholy, one feels emptiness where there might have been friendship and sublime and genuine affection, and one feels dreadful disappointment gnawing at one's spiritual energy [...] There may be a great fire in our soul, but no one ever comes to warm himself by it, all that passers-by can see is a little smoke coming out of the chimney, and they walk on. All right, then, what is to be done, should one tend that inward fire, turn to oneself for strength, wait patiently - yet with how much impatience! - wait, I say, for the moment when someone who wants to comes and sits down beside one's fire and perhaps stays on? [...]

What the moulting season is for birds - the time when they lose their feathers - setbacks, misfortune and hard times are for us human beings. You can cling on to the moulting season, you can also emerge from it reborn
source: WebExhibits 'Van Gogh's Letters' (letter 133 in the old numbering; 155 at vangoghletters.org). The page states the letter 'may be freely used, in accordance with the terms of this site.' | Letter to Theo, Cuesmes, June/July 1880
notes: Credit WebExhibits. The same letter contains a line about wanting to 'cease to be'; it has been cut and must stay out.

author: Oscar Wilde
title: De Profundis
primary_pairs: Sad › Guilty / Remorseful; Sad › Ashamed / Stupid
key_line: Where there is sorrow there is holy ground.
extract:
Suffering is one very long moment. We cannot divide it by seasons. We can only record its moods, and chronicle their return. With us time itself does not progress. It revolves. It seems to circle round one centre of pain. [...]

Where there is sorrow there is holy ground. Some day people will realise what that means. They will know nothing of life till they do.
source: De Profundis (Methuen, 1913), Project Gutenberg #921 | Opening; and the passage on sorrow

author: W. B. Yeats
title: Letter to Lady Elizabeth Pelham
secondary_pairs: Scared › Confused / Bewildered; Powerful › Important / Discerning
key_line: Man can embody truth but he cannot know it.
extract: [One line, then a retelling] "Man can embody truth but he cannot know it." Writing a few weeks before he died, Yeats told a friend that if he had to put everything he had learned into one phrase, it would be this: we never get to fully know what life means, but we can live it, and that is what he meant to do with the time he had left.
source: The Letters of W. B. Yeats, ed. Allan Wade (1954) | Letter of 4 January 1939

author: Mary Wollstonecraft
title: Letters Written During a Short Residence in Sweden, Norway, and Denmark
secondary_pairs: Peaceful › Loving / Serene; Mad › Critical / Skeptical
key_line: I was alone, till some involuntary sympathetic emotion [...] made me feel that I was still a part of a mighty whole
extract:
My child was sleeping with equal calmness--innocent and sweet as the closing flowers. Some recollections, attached to the idea of home, mingled with reflections respecting the state of society I had been contemplating that evening, made a tear drop on the rosy cheek I had just kissed [...]

How frequently has melancholy and even misanthropy taken possession of me, when the world has disgusted me, and friends have proved unkind. I have then considered myself as a particle broken off from the grand mass of mankind; I was alone, till some involuntary sympathetic emotion, like the attraction of adhesion, made me feel that I was still a part of a mighty whole, from which I could not sever myself
source: Letters Written During a Short Residence in Sweden, Norway, and Denmark (1796), Project Gutenberg #3529 | Letter I (night in Sweden)

author: Murasaki Shikibu
title: The Diary of Murasaki Shikibu
secondary_pairs: Sad › Depressed / Inferior; Mad › Hurt / Distant
key_line: I had passed my life without feeling any sort of contempt of myself until I went to Court
extract:
Although an unimportant person I had passed my life without feeling any sort of contempt of myself until I went to Court--since then, alas! I have experienced all the bitterness of it. [...]

Father, who was devoted to study, regretted that I had not been a son, but I heard people saying that it is not beautiful even for a man to be proud of his learning, and after that I did not write so much as the figure one in Chinese.
source: Diaries of Court Ladies of Old Japan, trans. Omori & Doi (1920), Project Gutenberg #47151 | The Diary of Murasaki Shikibu
notes: PD in the US. One translator died in 1979, so UK status is uncertain. Kept short; consider our own paraphrase for a public launch.

author: Li Qingzhao
title: Afterword to Records on Metal and Stone
primary_pairs: Sad › Lonely / Isolated; Peaceful › Thoughtful / Pensive
key_line: Yet where there is having there must be losing; what gathers together must scatter.
extract: Today I suddenly opened this book again, and it was like meeting an old friend. I remembered him in the hall at Donglai, the scrolls just newly mounted [...] Every evening, once the clerks had gone home, he would check two scrolls and write a note on one. [...] Now his handwriting looks as fresh as ever, yet the trees on his grave have already grown thick. How sad! [...] How hard these things were to gather, and how easily they were lost! Ah, from when I was eighteen until now, at fifty-two, in thirty-four years, how much worry and sorrow, how much gained and lost! Yet where there is having there must be losing; what gathers together must scatter. That is the ordinary way of things. Someone loses a bow, someone else finds it; why make so much of it?
source: Translated for this project from the Chinese original (金石錄後序, 1132), text via Chinese Wikisource | Closing section of the Afterword
notes: Ages follow the classical allusions in the text (Lu Ji at 20, minus two; Qu Boyu at 50, plus two).

author: Tao Yuanming (Tao Qian)
title: 'Return Home!' (Gui qu lai xi ci), with preface
secondary_pairs: Sad › Guilty / Remorseful; Peaceful › Content / Relaxed
key_line: Hunger and cold are real enough, but going against myself made me sick in body and mind.
extract:
My family was poor, and farming could not feed us. The house was full of small children and there was no grain in the jar. [...] So when a post came up in Pengze, a hundred li from home, I took it. But within a few days I felt a longing to go home. Why? My nature is what it is; it cannot be forced into another shape. Hunger and cold are real enough, but going against myself made me sick in body and mind. [...]

Return home! The fields and garden will soon be overgrown; why not go back?
I have made my mind the servant of my body; why be miserable and grieve alone?
I see now the past can't be put right, but I know the future can still be reached.
I have not gone so far down the wrong road; I can see today is right and yesterday was wrong.
source: Translated for this project from the Chinese original (歸去來兮辭并序, 405 CE), text via Chinese Wikisource | Prose preface, and the opening lines of the rhapsody

author: Abu Hamid al-Ghazali
title: Deliverance from Error (The Confessions of Al Ghazzali)
primary_pairs: Scared › Anxious / Overwhelmed; Scared › Confused / Bewildered
key_line: I advanced one step and immediately relapsed.
extract:
Still a prey to uncertainty, one day I decided to leave Bagdad and to give up everything; the next day I gave up my resolution. I advanced one step and immediately relapsed. [...] the Tempter, returning to the attack, said, "You are suffering from a transitory feeling; don't give way to it, for it will soon pass. If you obey it, if you give up this fine position, this honourable post exempt from trouble and rivalry, this seat of authority safe from attack, you will regret it later on without being able to recover it."

Thus I remained, torn asunder by the opposite forces of earthly passions and religious aspirations, for about six months [...] At the close of them my will yielded and I gave myself up to destiny. God caused an impediment to chain my tongue and prevented me from lecturing. Vainly I desired, in the interest of my pupils, to go on with my teaching, but my mouth became dumb.
source: The Confessions of Al Ghazzali, trans. Claud Field (1909), Project Gutenberg #58977 | Section 'Sufism'
notes: The following lines describe losing appetite and doctors fearing for his life; cut for the app.

author: Zahir-ud-din Muhammad Babur
title: Baburnama (Memoirs of Babur): the melon from Kabul
key_line: a melon was brought to me; to cut and eat it affected me strangely; I was all tears!
extract:
Boundless and infinite is my desire to go to those parts. [...]

How should a person forget the pleasant things of those countries, especially one who has repented and vowed to sin no more? How should he banish from his mind the permitted flavours of melons and grapes? Taking this opportunity, a melon was brought to me; to cut and eat it affected me strangely; I was all tears!
source: The Babur-nama in English, trans. Annette S. Beveridge (1922), Project Gutenberg #44608 | Copy of a letter to Khwaja Kalan (early 1529), quoted in the memoir
notes: Footnote markers removed. 'Repented' refers to his giving up wine.

author: M. K. Gandhi
title: An Autobiography, or The Story of My Experiments with Truth, Part II ch. 3 'The First Case'
primary_pairs: Scared › Insecure / Embarrassed; Sad › Ashamed / Stupid
secondary_pairs: Scared › Submissive / Inadequate; Scared › Anxious / Overwhelmed
key_line: I stood up, but my heart sank into my boots.
extract:
This was my debut in the Small Causes Court. I appeared for the defendant and had thus to cross-examine the plaintiff's witnesses. I stood up, but my heart sank into my boots. My head was reeling and I felt as though the whole court was doing likewise. I could think of no question to ask. The judge must have laughed and the vakils no doubt enjoyed the spectacle. But I was past seeing anything. I sat down and told the agent that I could not conduct the case [...]

I hastened from the Court, not knowing whether my client won or lost her case, but I was ashamed of myself, and decided not to take up any more cases until I had courage enough to conduct them.
source: An Autobiography, or The Story of My Experiments with Truth, trans. Mahadev Desai (Navajivan, 1927-29), via Internet Archive | Part II, chapter 3, 'The First Case'
notes: 'vakils' = court pleaders.

author: Rabindranath Tagore
title: Glimpses of Bengal (letters 1885-1895)
key_line: The world is so immense, the concourse of men so vast, yet with how few has one any tie!
extract:
Early this morning, while still lying in bed, I heard the women at the bathing-place sending forth joyous peals of Ulu! Ulu! The sound moved me curiously, though it is difficult to say why. Perhaps such joyful outbursts put one in mind of the great stream of festive activity which goes on in this world, with most of which the individual man has no connection. The world is so immense, the concourse of men so vast, yet with how few has one any tie! Distant sounds of life, wafted near, bearing tidings from unknown homes, make the individual realise that the greater part of the world of men does not, cannot own or know him; then he feels deserted, loosely attached to the world, and a vague sadness creeps over him. [...]

Each of the little joys of life, which remain unappreciated amid the hubbub of the town, send in their claims to the heart when far from home.
source: Glimpses of Bengal (Macmillan, 1921), Project Gutenberg #7951 | Letters from Shelidah, 22 June 1892, and Shazadpur, 25 June 1892
notes: 'Ulu! Ulu!' is a shrill festive cheer given by women.

author: Toru Dutt
title: Letters to Mary Martin
secondary_pairs: Sad › Bored / Apathetic; Mad › Critical / Skeptical
key_line: I have not been to one dinner party or any party at all since we left Europe.
extract: We do not go much into society now. The Bengali reunions are always for men. Wives and daughters and all womenkind are confined to the house, under lock and key, a la lettre! and Europeans are generally supercilious and look down on Bengalis. I have not been to one dinner party or any party at all since we left Europe. And then I do not know any people here, except those of our kith and kin, and some of them I do not know. [...] The life we lead here is so retired and quiet that I am afraid you find my letters dull.
source: Harihar Das, Life and Letters of Toru Dutt (OUP, 1921), via Internet Archive | Letter to Mary Martin, 1876
notes: Taken from an OCR scan: 'look down' was misread as 'look clown', and 'womenkind' is split across a line. Check both against the page image.

author: Kahlil Gibran
title: The Prophet, 'On Pain'
key_line: Your pain is the breaking of the shell that encloses your understanding.
extract:
And a woman spoke, saying, Tell us of Pain.

And he said:
Your pain is the breaking of the shell that encloses your understanding.
Even as the stone of the fruit must break, that its heart may stand in the sun, so must you know pain.
And could you keep your heart in wonder at the daily miracles of your life, your pain would not seem less wondrous than your joy;
And you would accept the seasons of your heart, even as you have always accepted the seasons that pass over your fields.
And you would watch with serenity through the winters of your grief.
source: The Prophet (Knopf, 1923), Project Gutenberg #58585 | 'On Pain'
notes: SAFETY: the section goes on to say 'Much of your pain is self-chosen'. Cut, because it could read as blame to someone struggling.

author: Olaudah Equiano
title: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, chapter 2
secondary_pairs: Scared › Helpless / Insignificant; Peaceful › Loving / Serene
key_line: thus for a while we forgot our misfortunes in the joy of being together
extract: In this manner I had been travelling for a considerable time, when one evening, to my great surprise, whom should I see brought to the house where I was but my dear sister! As soon as she saw me she gave a loud shriek, and ran into my arms--I was quite overpowered: neither of us could speak; but, for a considerable time, clung to each other in mutual embraces, unable to do any thing but weep. [...] and thus for a while we forgot our misfortunes in the joy of being together: but even this small comfort was soon to have an end; for scarcely had the fatal morning appeared, when she was again torn from me for ever!
source: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano (1789), Project Gutenberg #15399 | Chapter II

author: Mary Prince
title: The History of Mary Prince, a West Indian Slave
secondary_pairs: Powerful › Faithful / Confident; Mad › Critical / Skeptical
key_line: I have been a slave myself--I know what slaves feel
extract: All slaves want to be free--to be free is very sweet. I will say the truth to English people who may read this history that my good friend, Miss S----, is now writing down for me. I have been a slave myself--I know what slaves feel--I can tell by myself what other slaves feel, and by what they have told me. The man that says slaves be quite happy in slavery--that they don't want to be free--that man is either ignorant or a lying person. I never heard a slave say so.
source: The History of Mary Prince (1831), Project Gutenberg #17851 | Closing pages

author: Mary Seacole
title: Wonderful Adventures of Mrs Seacole in Many Lands
key_line: Did these ladies shrink from accepting my aid because my blood flowed beneath a somewhat duskier skin than theirs?
extract: [...] one cold evening I stood in the twilight, which was fast deepening into wintry night, and looked back upon the ruins of my last castle in the air. The disappointment seemed a cruel one. I was so conscious of the unselfishness of the motives which induced me to leave England--so certain of the service I could render among the sick soldiery, and yet I found it so difficult to convince others of these facts. Doubts and suspicions arose in my heart for the first and last time, thank Heaven. Was it possible that American prejudices against colour had some root here? Did these ladies shrink from accepting my aid because my blood flowed beneath a somewhat duskier skin than theirs? Tears streamed down my foolish cheeks, as I stood in the fast thinning streets; tears of grief that any should doubt my motives--that Heaven should deny me the opportunity that I sought. Then I stood still, and looking upward through and through the dark clouds that shadowed London, prayed aloud for help.
source: Wonderful Adventures of Mrs. Seacole in Many Lands (1857), Project Gutenberg #23031 | Chapter VIII (applying to go to the Crimea)
notes: Chapter number to verify.

author: Frederick Douglass
title: Letter to Thomas Auld
secondary_pairs: Mad › Angry / Frustrated; Powerful › Faithful / Confident
key_line: I am your fellow-man, but not your slave.
extract:
I am myself; you are yourself; we are two distinct persons, equal persons. What you are, I am. You are a man, and so am I. God created both, and made us separate beings. [...]

In doing this, I entertain no malice toward you personally. There is no roof under which you would be more safe than mine, and there is nothing in my house which you might need for your comfort, which I would not readily grant. [...] I am your fellow-man, but not your slave.
source: Letter 'To My Old Master, Thomas Auld' (1848), reprinted in My Bondage and My Freedom (1855), Project Gutenberg #202 | Appendix: 'Letter to his old master'

author: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
title: Reply to Sister Filotea (Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz)
secondary_pairs: Mad › Angry / Frustrated; Powerful › Faithful / Confident
key_line: no punishments or scoldings were enough to stop me.
extract: When I was about six or seven, and could already read and write, along with all the needlework and sewing that women are taught, I heard that in Mexico City there was a University, and schools where the sciences were studied. No sooner had I heard it than I began to wear my mother out with constant, pestering pleas to change my clothes [dress me as a boy] and send me to Mexico City, to some relatives she had there, so that I could study and attend the University. She wouldn't do it, and she was quite right; but I satisfied the longing by reading the many books my grandfather owned, and no punishments or scoldings were enough to stop me.

author: Emily Dickinson
title: First letter to Thomas Wentworth Higginson
secondary_pairs: Scared › Submissive / Inadequate; Joyful › Creative / Playful
key_line: Are you too deeply occupied to say if my verse is alive?
extract:
Mr Higginson,--Are you too deeply occupied to say if my verse is alive?

The mind is so near itself it cannot see distinctly, and I have none to ask.

Should you think it breathed, and had you the leisure to tell me, I should feel quick gratitude.

If I make the mistake, that you dared to tell me would give me sincerer honor toward you.

I enclose my name, asking you, if you please, sir, to tell me what is true?

That you will not betray me it is needless to ask, since honor is its own pawn.
source: Letters of Emily Dickinson, ed. Mabel Loomis Todd (1894), via Internet Archive | To T. W. Higginson (dated there April 16, 1862; usually dated 15 April)
notes: Todd's 1894 text normalises Dickinson's capitals ('Verse' in the manuscript).

author: Abraham Lincoln
title: Letter to Fanny McCullough
secondary_pairs: Peaceful › Nurturing / Thankful; Sad › Depressed / Inferior
key_line: You are sure to be happy again.
extract:
It is with deep regret that I learn of the death of your kind and brave father, and especially that it is affecting your young heart beyond what is common in such cases. In this sad world of ours sorrow comes to all, and to the young it comes with bittered [usually printed 'bitterest'] agony because it takes them unawares.

The older have learned ever to expect it. I am anxious to afford some alleviation of your present distress, perfect relief is not possible, except with time. You cannot now realize that you will ever feel better. Is not this so? And yet it is a mistake. You are sure to be happy again. To know this, which is certainly true, will make you some less miserable now. I have had experience enough to know what I say, and you need only to believe it to feel better at once. The memory of your dear father, instead of an agony, will yet be a sad, sweet feeling in your heart, of a purer and holier sort than you have known before.
source: The Papers and Writings of Abraham Lincoln, vol. 6 (Constitutional ed.), Project Gutenberg #2658 | Letter to Miss Fanny McCullough, 23 December 1862
notes: Gutenberg text reads 'bittered'; most printings read 'bitterest'. Check against a facsimile and choose one.

author: Zitkala-Ša (Gertrude Simmons Bonnin)
title: The School Days of an Indian Girl, 'The Cutting of My Long Hair'
secondary_pairs: Mad › Angry / Frustrated; Joyful › Excited / Daring
key_line: "No, I will not submit! I will struggle first!"
extract:
Late in the morning, my friend Judéwin gave me a terrible warning. Judéwin knew a few words of English; and she had overheard the paleface woman talk about cutting our long, heavy hair. Our mothers had taught us that only unskilled warriors who were captured had their hair shingled by the enemy. Among our people, short hair was worn by mourners, and shingled hair by cowards!

We discussed our fate some moments, and when Judéwin said, "We have to submit, because they are strong," I rebelled.

"No, I will not submit! I will struggle first!" I answered. [...]

I cried aloud, shaking my head all the while until I felt the cold blades of the scissors against my neck, and heard them gnaw off one of my thick braids. Then I lost my spirit. Since the day I was taken from my mother I had suffered extreme indignities. People had stared at me. I had been tossed about in the air like a wooden puppet. And now my long hair was shingled like a coward's! In my anguish I moaned for my mother, but no one came to comfort me.
source: American Indian Stories (1921), Project Gutenberg #10376 | The School Days of an Indian Girl, II, 'The Cutting of My Long Hair'
notes: Opening words 'Late in the morning, my friend' checked against a second transcription.

author: Woollarawarre Bennelong
title: Letter to Mr Phillips, Lord Sydney's steward
primary_pairs: Peaceful › Content / Relaxed; Peaceful › Trusting / Secure
key_line: Not me go to England no more. I am at home now.
extract: All my friends alive and well. Not me go to England no more. I am at home now. I hope Mrs Phillips is very well. You nurse me madam when I sick. You very good madam; thank you madam, and hope you remember me madam, not forget. I know you very well madam. Madam, I want stockings, thank you madam. Send me two pair of stockings.
source: Letter of 29 August 1796, National Library of Australia MS 4005 (transcription as published by AIATSIS) | Middle of the letter
notes: Assembled from two published transcriptions that agree. Check against NLA's digitised manuscript.

author: Jane Austen
title: Letters to her sister Cassandra
key_line: I do not want people to be very agreeable, as it saves me the trouble of liking them a great deal.
extract:
Miss Blackford is agreeable enough. I do not want people to be very agreeable, as it saves me the trouble of liking them a great deal.

[...]

Mr. Richard Harvey is going to be married; but as it is a great secret, and only known to half the neighborhood, you must not mention it.
source: The Letters of Jane Austen, ed. Sarah Chauncey Woolsey (1892), Project Gutenberg #42078 | Letter from Steventon, 24 December [1798]; letter from Rowling, 18 September [1796]
notes: Years in square brackets come from the edition's ordering; check the Rowling letter's year (1796).

author: Samuel Pepys
title: Diary entry for 15 May 1663
key_line: it is a deadly folly and plague that I bring upon myself to be so jealous
extract: [...] and so well pleased home, where I found it almost night, and my wife and the dancing-master alone above, not dancing but talking. Now so deadly full of jealousy I am that my heart and head did so cast about and fret that I could not do any business possibly, but went out to my office, and anon late home again and ready to chide at every thing, and then suddenly to bed and could hardly sleep, yet durst not say any thing [...] But it is a deadly folly and plague that I bring upon myself to be so jealous
source: Diary of Samuel Pepys, 1663 (Wheatley edition), Project Gutenberg #4145 | Entry for 15 May 1663
notes: One clause describing the dancing master's appearance has been cut.

author: Marcus Aurelius
title: Meditations, Book II
key_line: for we are all born to be fellow-workers, as the feet, the hands, and the eyelids
extract: Betimes in the morning say to thyself, This day I shalt have to do with an idle curious man, with an unthankful man, a railer, a crafty, false, or an envious man; an unsociable uncharitable man. All these ill qualities have happened unto them, through ignorance of that which is truly good and truly bad. [...] How can I either be hurt by any of those, since it is not in their power to make me incur anything that is truly reproachful? or angry, and ill affected towards him, who by nature is so near unto me? for we are all born to be fellow-workers, as the feet, the hands, and the eyelids; as the rows of the upper and under teeth
source: Meditations, trans. Meric Casaubon (1634), Project Gutenberg #2680 | Book II, opening
notes: 17th-century translation: 'I shalt' is as printed. 'Betimes' = early.

author: Michel de Montaigne
title: Of Cannibals
key_line: every one gives the title of barbarism to everything that is not in use in his own country.
extract: I find that there is nothing barbarous and savage in this nation, by anything that I can gather, excepting, that every one gives the title of barbarism to everything that is not in use in his own country. As, indeed, we have no other level of truth and reason than the example and idea of the opinions and customs of the place wherein we live: there is always the perfect religion, there the perfect government, there the most exact and accomplished usage of all things.
source: Essays of Michel de Montaigne, trans. Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, Project Gutenberg #3600 | Book I, 'Of Cannibals'

author: John Keats
title: Letter to Charles Wentworth Dilke
key_line: good God how fine.
extract: Talking of Pleasure, this moment I was writing with one hand, and with the other holding to my Mouth a Nectarine--good God how fine. It went down soft, pulpy, slushy, oozy--all its delicious embonpoint melted down my throat like a large beatified Strawberry.
source: Letters of John Keats to His Family and Friends, ed. Sidney Colvin (1891), Project Gutenberg #35698 | Letter CXVIII, to C. W. Dilke, Winchester, 22 September 1819
notes: 'embonpoint' = plumpness.

author: Matsuo Bashō
title: The Narrow Road to the Deep North (Oku no Hosomichi), opening
key_line: the gods of the road beckoned, and I couldn't keep my mind on anything.
extract: The months and days are travellers of a hundred ages, and the years that come and go are travellers too. Those who spend their lives on boats, or grow old leading horses by the bridle, make every day a journey and make the journey their home. [...] I too, for some years now, have been drawn by the wind like a scrap of cloud, and could not stop longing to wander. [...] When spring came with its haze, I wanted to cross the Shirakawa barrier. The spirit of restlessness took hold of me and set my heart racing; the gods of the road beckoned, and I couldn't keep my mind on anything. I patched my trousers, put a new cord on my hat, and before I'd even finished treating my legs for the walk, the moon over Matsushima was already filling my thoughts.
source: Translated for this project from the Japanese original, text via Japanese Wikisource | Opening section
notes: A line about ancient poets dying on the road has been cut. 'Treating my legs' refers to moxa, a traditional heat treatment for travellers.

author: Ignatius Sancho
title: Letter IX, to Mr K----
key_line: all was soon to rights--nothing broke--and no one hurt--and laughter had its fill.
extract:
We came home from our Highland excursion last Monday night, safe and well--after escaping manifold dangers.--Mesdames H----, D----, and self, went into the post-coach, and were honour'd with the freedom of Dumbarton. By an overset, the ladies shewed their--delicacy--and I my activity--Mr. B---- his humanity;--all was soon to rights--nothing broke--and no one hurt--and laughter had its fill.--Inverary is a charming place--the beauties various--and the whole plan majestic;--there are some worthy souls on the spot, which I admire more than the buildings and prospects.--We had herrings in perfection--and would have had mackarel; but the scoundrels were too sharp for us--and would not be caught.

[The 1782 editor's footnote: Mr. Sancho was remarkably unwieldy and inactive, and never gave a greater proof of it than at this overset, when he and a goose-pye were equally incapable of raising themselves.]
source: Letters of the Late Ignatius Sancho, an African (1782), Project Gutenberg #66908 | Letter IX, Dalkeith, 16 July 1770
notes: 'overset' = the coach overturning. Check the voting claim before using it on screen.

author: Vincent van Gogh
title: Letter to Theo van Gogh, 14 August 1882
secondary_pairs: Joyful › Energetic / Stimulating; Powerful › Aware / Surprised
key_line: it is only to tell you that painting is such a joy to me.
extract:
You must not take it amiss if I write you again - it is only to tell you that painting is such a joy to me. [...]

To tell you the truth, it surprises me a little. I had expected the first things to be a failure, though I supposed they would improve later on; but though I say so myself, they are not bad at all, and I repeat, it surprises me a little. [...]

I simply couldn't restrain myself or keep my hands off it or allow myself any rest.
source: WebExhibits 'Van Gogh's Letters', letter 225 (trans. Johanna van Gogh-Bonger, ed. Robert Harrison) | Letter 225, The Hague, 14 August 1882

author: Charlotte Brontë
title: Letter to her sister Emily
secondary_pairs: Scared › Helpless / Insignificant; Mad › Hurt / Distant
key_line: it is dreary work to look on and listen.
extract: I have striven hard to be pleased with my new situation. The country, the house and the grounds are, as I have said, divine; but, alack-a-day! there is such a thing as seeing all beautiful around you--pleasant woods, white paths, green lawns, and blue sunshiny sky--and not having a free moment or a free thought left to enjoy them. [...] she cares nothing about me, except to contrive how the greatest possible quantity of labour may be got out of me; and to that end she overwhelms me with oceans of needle-work; yards of cambric to hem, muslin nightcaps to make, and, above all things, dolls to dress. [...] I used to think I should like to be in the stir of grand folks' society; but I have had enough of it--it is dreary work to look on and listen. I see more clearly than I have ever done before, that a private governess has no existence, is not considered as a living rational being, except as connected with the wearisome duties she has to fulfil
source: Elizabeth Gaskell, The Life of Charlotte Brontë, vol. 1 (1857), Project Gutenberg #1827 | Letter to Emily Brontë, 8 June 1839

author: Elizabeth Barrett Barrett
title: Reply to Robert Browning's first letter
primary_pairs: Peaceful › Intimate / Responsive; Peaceful › Nurturing / Thankful
key_line: the exchange of sympathy for gratitude is the most princely thing!
extract: I thank you, dear Mr. Browning, from the bottom of my heart. You meant to give me pleasure by your letter--and even if the object had not been answered, I ought still to thank you. But it is thoroughly answered. Such a letter from such a hand! Sympathy is dear--very dear to me: but the sympathy of a poet, and of such a poet, is the quintessence of sympathy to me! Will you take back my gratitude for it?--agreeing, too, that of all the commerce done in the world, from Tyre to Carthage, the exchange of sympathy for gratitude is the most princely thing!
source: The Letters of Robert Browning and Elizabeth Barrett Barrett, vol. 1 (1899), Project Gutenberg #16182 | E.B.B. to R.B., 50 Wimpole Street, 11 January 1845

author: Julian of Norwich
title: Revelations of Divine Love, chapter 27
key_line: all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well.
extract: And thus, in my folly, afore this time often I wondered why by the great foreseeing wisdom of God the beginning of sin was not letted: for then, methought, all should have been well. [...] But Jesus, who in this Vision informed me of all that is needful to me, answered by this word and said: It behoved that there should be sin; but all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well. [...] All this was shewed in a touch and quickly passed over into comfort
source: Revelations of Divine Love, ed. Grace Warrack (1901), Project Gutenberg #52958 | The Thirteenth Revelation, chapter XXVII
notes: 'letted' = prevented.

author: Frederick Douglass
title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, chapter VI
key_line: From that moment, I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom.
extract: These words sank deep into my heart, stirred up sentiments within that lay slumbering, and called into existence an entirely new train of thought. It was a new and special revelation, explaining dark and mysterious things, with which my youthful understanding had struggled, but struggled in vain. [...] It was a grand achievement, and I prized it highly. From that moment, I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom. It was just what I wanted, and I got it at a time when I the least expected it.
source: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (1845), Project Gutenberg #23 | Chapter VI
notes: The preceding speech by his enslaver contains slurs and is not shown; the summary explains it.

author: Booker T. Washington
title: Up from Slavery, chapter III
key_line: The sweeping of that room was my college examination
extract:
After some hours had passed, the head teacher said to me: "The adjoining recitation-room needs sweeping. Take the broom and sweep it."

It occurred to me at once that here was my chance. Never did I receive an order with more delight. [...]

I swept the recitation-room three times. Then I got a dusting-cloth and dusted it four times. [...] When she was unable to find one bit of dirt on the floor, or a particle of dust on any of the furniture, she quietly remarked, "I guess you will do to enter this institution."

I was one of the happiest souls on Earth. The sweeping of that room was my college examination, and never did any youth pass an examination for entrance into Harvard or Yale that gave him more genuine satisfaction.
source: Up from Slavery (1901), Project Gutenberg #2376 | Chapter III, 'The Struggle for an Education'

author: Mary Seacole
title: Wonderful Adventures of Mrs Seacole in Many Lands: meeting at Gibraltar
key_line: "Do you think I shall be of any use to you when I get there?" "Surely."
extract:
"And you are going to the front, old lady--you, of all people in the world?"

"Why not, my sons?--won't they be glad to have me there?"

"By Jove! yes, mother," answered one, an Irishman. "It isn't many women--God bless them!--we've had to spoil us out there. But it's not the place even for you, who know what hardship is." [...]

"Do you think I shall be of any use to you when I get there?"

"Surely."

"Then I'll go, were the place a hundred times worse than you describe it."
source: Wonderful Adventures of Mrs. Seacole in Many Lands (1857), Project Gutenberg #23031 | Chapter on the voyage out (Gibraltar)

author: José Martí
title: Our America (Nuestra América)
secondary_pairs: Joyful › Creative / Playful; Powerful › Proud / Successful
key_line: Wine made from plantains; and if it comes out sour, it's our wine!
extract:
Let the world be grafted onto our republics; but the trunk must be our own. [...]

Peoples are getting to their feet and greeting one another. "What are we like?" they ask, and they begin telling each other what they are like. When a problem comes up in Cojímar, they don't go looking for the answer in Danzig. The frock coats are still French, but the thinking is beginning to be our own. The young people of America are rolling their sleeves up to the elbow, plunging their hands into the dough and making it rise with the yeast of their own sweat. They understand that there is too much imitation, and that salvation lies in creating. Create is this generation's password. Wine made from plantains; and if it comes out sour, it's our wine!
source: Translated for this project from the Spanish original (1891), text via Spanish Wikisource | Middle section
notes: 'America' here means Latin America; we rendered one instance as 'our own' to make that clear. Cojímar is a Cuban fishing village; Danzig a European port.
